meta.title: Smart Workout Optimizer (SWO): exercise-level training guidance
meta.description: Wearable-free training guidance. SWO turns sleep quality, fatigue and workout history into exercise-level Green, Amber and Red recommendations.

hero.headline: Training decisions, without the guesswork.
hero.supportingCopy: Tell SWO three things before you lift: how you slept, how fatigued or stiff you feel, and what you have been training. It turns those into Green, Amber and Red guidance for each exercise, with the reasoning shown beside every call. No wearable required.

preview.alt: SWO daily screen showing an optimal-zone readiness score of 73, a start-session button, and a training-load chart plotting ACWR against daily load across a week
preview.caption: The SWO app's daily screen.

problem.heading: The hardest rep is the first decision
problem.body: Choosing today's weights from memory and mood is easy. Holding sleep, soreness and last week's sessions in your head at once, and deciding what they add up to while you are standing at the rack, is much harder.
points: A short night changes how a session goes, but by how much is a guess.
Stiffness from two days ago is easy to notice and easy to ignore.
Last session's numbers are rarely remembered as accurately as they feel.

howItWorks.heading: Three inputs, then a call on every exercise
howItWorks.intro: SWO reads what you tell it, considers it alongside established training concepts, and answers per exercise rather than for the day as a whole.

steps.title: Record your sleep quality
steps.description: Rate how well you slept before you train. It takes a moment and needs no device on your wrist.

steps.title: Assess fatigue and stiffness
steps.description: Note how tired or stiff you feel today, so the guidance reflects the state you are actually in.

steps.title: Your workout history
steps.description: The sets and reps you log build up the recent training context, so nothing depends on recall.

steps.title: SWO reads it against training concepts
steps.description: Your inputs are considered alongside workload, recovery and progression ideas drawn from sports science.

steps.title: You get a call you can argue with
steps.description: Each exercise gets a state, the reasoning behind it and a suggested action, so you can judge it rather than obey it.

statusSection.heading: Green, Amber and Red, explained
statusSection.intro: Each exercise gets one of three states. The colour is a shorthand; the label, the icon and the reasoning are what carry the meaning, and all three appear together everywhere they are used.

image.alt: End-of-session list of eight exercises, each with a written state beside it: seven read GREEN and Dumbbell Shoulder Press reads RED
image.caption: States appear as words in the app, not only as colours.

statuses.label: Optimal zone
statuses.meaning: The exercise sits inside the training range SWO has worked out for you today.
statuses.exampleRationale: Example: recovery looks strong and you have held steady on this exercise for several sessions, so there is room to ask for a little more.
statuses.suggestedAction: Train as planned, or take the suggested step up in load or reps.

statuses.label: Caution zone
statuses.meaning: Something in today's inputs suggests the intensity or the volume is worth adjusting.
statuses.exampleRationale: Example: the muscle itself is recovered, but overall readiness is only moderate, so a lighter session may get more out of the day.
statuses.suggestedAction: Consider dropping the weight or cutting a set, and see how the first working set feels.

statuses.label: High-risk flag
statuses.meaning: SWO's rules point towards rest or active recovery for this exercise today.
statuses.exampleRationale: Example: recovery signals and recent training load both point the same way, towards holding back on this particular lift.
statuses.suggestedAction: Rest it, or swap in an active-recovery option and come back to it next session.

featureSection.heading: What this looks like in the app
featureSection.intro: Every screen below is the real interface. Nothing here is a mock-up, and this page is a preview rather than a live connection to the app.

features.heading: A call on every exercise, not one score for the day
features.description: A good day for your legs can hide a poor day for your shoulders. SWO gives each exercise its own state, so you adjust the lift that needs it and leave the rest of the session alone.
bullets: Every state is shown as a word and an icon, never as colour alone.
Suggested next-set targets sit beside the reasoning, not instead of it.

image.alt: Exercise card for a lying leg curl marked as an optimal day to progress, with two suggested next-set targets and the sets logged underneath

features.heading: The reasoning sits next to the recommendation
features.description: When SWO suggests easing off, it says why in plain words and offers a specific lighter target. You can disagree with it, which is the point: it is there to inform the decision, not to make it for you.

image.alt: Exercise card in the caution zone, explaining in a sentence why a reduced weight is suggested and offering a lighter set to try

features.heading: Open up any assessment and see what went into it
features.description: The daily readiness figure is not a black box. Tapping it breaks out the parts it was built from, including your sleep and energy ratings and where your recent workload sits.
bullets: Each input is shown with the value you gave it.
Unusual entries, such as a sudden jump in weight, are called out separately.

image.alt: Why this score panel breaking a readiness figure into sleep and energy ratings and an acute-to-chronic workload ratio, with a note about an unusually large weight increase

features.heading: Progress when the day supports it
features.description: On a day its rules judge suitable, SWO proposes a specific next step rather than a vague instruction to push. On a day that does not look suitable, it proposes nothing and says so.

image.alt: Exercise card flagged as an optimal day to progress, offering two concrete next-set targets above the logged sets for the exercise

methodology.heading: The ideas behind the guidance
methodology.intro: SWO draws on established training concepts. Each one is described here twice on purpose: first as the concept itself, then as what this app actually does with it. The two are not the same thing, and the difference matters.
methodology.unsourcedNotice: Described as a training concept. No study is cited here, and none is implied.

frameworks.name: Acute-to-chronic workload ratio
frameworks.concept: A published way of comparing the training load of the last few days with the load an athlete has been used to over a longer stretch. It is widely discussed in sports science, and its usefulness as an individual-level indicator is debated rather than settled.
frameworks.swoImplementation: SWO calculates this ratio from your logged sessions and uses it as one input among several when it forms guidance. It is not treated as a verdict on its own, and this page does not claim it forecasts injury.

frameworks.name: Fatigue and recovery
frameworks.concept: The idea that training produces fatigue, that recovery resolves it over time, and that how ready you are on a given day reflects the balance between the two.
frameworks.swoImplementation: SWO asks you to rate sleep quality and how fatigued or stiff you feel, and reflects those ratings in the day's guidance. It uses what you report; it does not measure your physiology.

frameworks.name: Progressive overload
frameworks.concept: Gradually increasing the demand placed on the body over time, for example a small increase in load or one more repetition, as the basis for getting stronger.
frameworks.swoImplementation: When its rules judge a day suitable, SWO suggests a specific next target such as a slightly heavier load or an extra rep, based on what you have recently lifted on that exercise.

methodology.disclaimer: SWO is a training decision-support tool. It does not diagnose, treat or prevent injury or illness, and it is not a substitute for advice from a qualified professional. Its guidance follows the app's own rules applied to what you report, and has not been clinically validated. Treat it as one more thing to weigh up, alongside how you actually feel.

audiences.heading: Who this is for
audiences.intro: SWO is built first for people making their own training decisions, and is useful second as a shared reference point between a coach and the person they train.

groups.name: Individual gym-goers and serious lifters
groups.description: If you train regularly without a coach in the room, you are making the load and volume calls yourself, session after session. SWO gives those calls a consistent starting point instead of a fresh guess each time.
points: A reasoned starting position for each exercise before you warm up.
A record of what you lifted, so progression is based on numbers rather than memory.
A reason attached to every suggestion, so you can overrule it knowingly.

groups.name: Coaches and personal trainers
groups.description: Conversations about readiness and progression are easier with something concrete in front of you. SWO gives a client's reported sleep, fatigue and recent load a shared shape you can both look at between sessions.
points: A common vocabulary for readiness that a client already understands.
Visible reasoning, so a suggestion can be discussed rather than taken on trust.

image.alt: A person performing a seated lat pulldown on a cable machine in a gym, seen from behind
image.caption: Built around how people actually train, not around a device.

faqSection.heading: Questions people ask first
faqSection.intro: Short answers about what SWO needs from you, what it gives back, and the things it deliberately does not claim to do.

faq.question: Do I need a smartwatch or a wearable?
faq.answer: No. SWO is wearable-free by design. It works from three things you provide yourself: how well you slept, how fatigued or stiff you feel, and the workouts you log in the app.

faq.question: What information does SWO actually use?
faq.answer: Your sleep-quality rating, your fatigue and stiffness rating, and your workout performance history from the sessions you have logged. It considers those alongside training concepts such as workload balance, recovery and progressive overload. It does not read any physiological measurement from a device.

faq.question: What do the three guidance states mean?
faq.answer: Green marks an exercise as sitting in the optimal zone for today. Amber is a caution zone, where adjusting the weight or the number of sets may be worthwhile. Red is a high-risk flag, where the app's rules point towards rest or active recovery for that exercise. Every state appears with a written label, a distinct icon and the reasoning behind it.

faq.question: Can SWO stop me getting hurt?
faq.answer: No. SWO does not predict or prevent injury, and no honest tool can promise that. It is a decision-support app: it organises what you have told it and offers a reasoned suggestion. Whether to follow that suggestion remains your judgement.

faq.question: Is SWO a replacement for professional medical advice?
faq.answer: No. SWO is not medical advice and does not diagnose anything. If you have pain, an existing condition or any concern about training, speak to a qualified professional. Nothing on this page or in the app replaces that.

faq.question: Are the screenshots on this page a live product?
faq.answer: The screenshots show the real SWO interface, captured from the app. This page is a marketing preview of it, not a connection to a running account, and the figures shown are from the captured sessions.

finalCta.heading: Start with the reasoning, not the verdict
finalCta.body: The clearest way to judge SWO is to look at how it reaches a call and decide whether that reasoning is one you would use yourself.

footer.legalNote: SWO is a training decision-support tool, not medical advice. Screenshots show the app interface and do not represent a live connection. Guidance follows the app's own rules applied to what you report.
